adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Before the thirteenth century most Europeans measured the passing of hours with water clocks, sand glasses, or the slow burning of candles marked at intervals. These devices were unreliable, since water could freeze, sand could clump after damp weather, and a draught could make a flame gutter and burn faster than its owner expected. Monasteries needed something better, because the round of prayer demanded that someone wake the community at fixed hours regardless of season or cloud cover.

The first weight-driven clocks appeared in the bell towers of Italian and English cathedrals late in the thirteenth century. A heavy stone or iron weight, suspended on a rope wound around a drum, turned a train of wooden wheels as it descended. An escapement, at first a simple bar with pins that caught the teeth of the last wheel, released the train one tooth at a time and produced the steady tick that gave the machine its name. The word itself came from the Latin word for a bell, since the earliest examples announced the hour by striking rather than by showing a dial.

Craftsmen soon discovered that a clock kept poor time if its wheels were cut by eye. Each wheel had to mesh with its neighbour, and every tooth had to be shaped so that the push it gave was even. By the fifteenth century the best workshops in Nuremberg and Augsburg were cutting brass wheels with dividing engines, and clocks had shrunk from room-sized tower machines to table ornaments that a merchant could own.

Spring-driven clocks brought a new problem. A weight pulls with constant force, but a coiled spring pulls hardest when fully wound and weakly when nearly spent. Clockmakers solved this with the fusee, a cone-shaped pulley whose changing radius compensated for the fading spring. The fusee remained standard equipment for three hundred years, until the pendulum and the anchor escapement made accuracy depend less on the driving force and more on the regularity of a swinging bob.

A good pendulum clock could hold to a few seconds a day, which was enough to expose a further difficulty: metals expand when warm. A steel rod lengthened on a sunny afternoon and shortened again at night, and the clock ran slow in the heat and fast in the cold. Gridiron pendulums, mercury compensation jars, and eventually invar rods each attacked this error, and each taught makers that a timekeeper is only as good as the materials from which it is built.

None of these improvements came quickly. Each generation of clockmakers inherited a machine that was slightly better than the one before it, and each generation found a new source of error hiding inside the accuracy that the last had won.
